title: R and Python Analysis of Penguin Body Mass
text:
The Palmer Penguins dataset contains measurements collected from penguins observed near Palmer Station in Antarctica. In this analysis, I use both R and Python in the same Quarto document.
The R code prepares the data and calculates species-level summaries. The Python code receives data from R, performs an additional calculation, and returns the result to R.
Data source: Palmer Penguins, created by Allison Horst using data from Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
The dataset is distributed with the palmerpenguins package, so the analysis does not need to download a data file from the internet during rendering.

The R code prepares the data and calculates species-level summaries. The Python code receives data from R, performs an additional calculation, and returns the result to R.

The dataset is distributed with the palmerpenguins package, so the analysis does not need to download a data file from the internet during rendering.

title: R and Python Analysis of Penguin Body Mass
section: Load and prepare the data in R
text:
Load and prepare the data in R
First, I load the Palmer Penguins data in R and remove observations that are missing body mass or species.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(reticulate)

analysis_data <- penguins %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(species),
    !is.na(body_mass_g)
  )

cat("Rows after cleaning:", nrow(analysis_data), "\n")

Rows after cleaning: 342 

head(analysis_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
5 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
6 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181        3625
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>


The cleaned dataset contains the observations needed for the analysis.

title: R and Python Analysis of Penguin Body Mass
text:
Calculate species means in R
I calculate the mean body mass for each penguin species.

r_summary <- analysis_data %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_body_mass_g = round(mean_body_mass_g, 1)
  )

r_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   observations mean_body_mass_g
  <fct>            <int>            <dbl>
1 Adelie             151            3701.
2 Chinstrap           68            3733.
3 Gentoo             123            5076 


The R calculation produces a species-level summary that will be passed to Python.

title: R and Python Analysis of Penguin Body Mass
section: Pass the R result to Python
text:
Pass the R result to Python
The reticulate package allows R and Python to communicate within the same Quarto document.
I pass the cleaned R data to Python as a pandas DataFrame. Python then calculates the overall mean body mass.

import pandas as pd

python_data = r.analysis_data

overall_mean = float(python_data["body_mass_g"].mean())

print("Python received", len(python_data), "observations")

Python received 342 observations

print(f"Overall mean body mass: {overall_mean:.1f} g")

Overall mean body mass: 4201.8 g


The Python code receives the object created in R and calculates a new result from it.

title: R and Python Analysis of Penguin Body Mass
section: Pass the Python result back to R
text:
Pass the Python result back to R
The Python result can also be accessed from R.

python_mean <- py$overall_mean

cat(
  "Overall mean body mass calculated by Python:",
  round(python_mean, 1),
  "g\n"
)

Overall mean body mass calculated by Python: 4201.8 g


This demonstrates the two-way workflow: R creates the data object, Python uses that object to calculate a result, and R reads the Python result.

title: R and Python Analysis of Penguin Body Mass
text:
Visualize the data in Python
Finally, I use the Python DataFrame to create a figure showing body mass by species.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

python_data.boxplot(
    column="body_mass_g",
    by="species",
    ax=ax
)

ax.axhline(
    overall_mean,
    color="black",
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=1.5,
    label=f"Overall mean: {overall_mean:.0f} g"
)

ax.set_title("Penguin Body Mass by Species")
ax.set_xlabel("Species")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.legend()

plt.suptitle("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Penguin body mass by species, using data prepared in R and visualized in Python.

title: R and Python Analysis of Penguin Body Mass
text:
Findings
The analysis demonstrates how R and Python can be used together in one Quarto document.
R was used to load and clean the Palmer Penguins data and calculate species-level summaries. The cleaned R data were then passed to Python, where the overall mean body mass was calculated.
The Python result was subsequently accessed from R, demonstrating that objects can be passed between the two languages through reticulate.
The figure shows differences in body mass among the three penguin species, along with the overall mean body mass across the cleaned observations.
These are descriptive results from the Palmer Penguins dataset and do not establish causal relationships.

title: R and Python Analysis of Penguin Body Mass
text:
Conclusion
This post demonstrates a reproducible mixed-language workflow using R, Python, Quarto, and reticulate. The same computational document contains R and Python code, passes an object from R to Python, performs a calculation in Python, and passes the resulting value back to R.
Because all calculations and the figure are generated during rendering, the analysis can be reproduced from the project environment rather than relying on manually created outputs.

title: Penguin Body Mass Across Species
text:
Findings
The summary statistics and figure show that body mass differs among the three penguin species.
Gentoo penguins are much heavier than the other two species, averaging about 5,076 g, while Adelie (about 3,701 g) and Chinstrap (about 3,733 g) penguins have very similar average body masses (Table 1). The boxplots in Figure 1 show the same pattern, and also that the Adelie and Chinstrap distributions overlap almost completely.
These are descriptive patterns in the Palmer Penguins dataset. This analysis does not perform a statistical hypothesis test or attempt to generalize beyond the observations represented by these data.

title: Penguin Body Mass Across Species
text:
Conclusion
Using Python, I loaded the Palmer Penguins dataset, inspected its structure, removed observations with missing values for the variables of interest, calculated species-level body-mass summaries, and created a visualization of the distributions.
This provides a reproducible computational workflow in Python because the data loading, cleaning, summary calculations, and visualization are all performed by code when the Quarto document is rendered.

title: Flipper Length and Body Mass in Penguins
text:
The Palmer Penguins dataset contains measurements collected from penguins observed near Palmer Station in Antarctica. In this analysis, I examine the relationship between flipper length and body mass across the three penguin species.
The goal is to summarize the measurements by species and visualize the relationship between flipper length and body mass.
Data source: Palmer Penguins, created by Allison Horst using data from Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

title: Flipper Length and Body Mass in Penguins
text:
Load and inspect the data
The dataset is provided by the palmerpenguins R package, so the analysis does not require downloading a data file from the internet at render time.

library(palmerpenguins)

penguins_data <- penguins

Prepare the data

title: Flipper Length and Body Mass in Penguins
text:
Summarize by species
I calculate the number of observations, mean flipper length, mean body mass, and the correlation between the two measurements for each species.

species_summary <- analysis_data %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    mean_flipper_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g),
    correlation = cor(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(mean_flipper_mm, mean_body_mass_g, correlation),
      ~ round(.x, 2)
    )
  )

knitr::kable(species_summary)

title: Flipper Length and Body Mass in Penguins
text:
Visualize the relationship
The following figure plots body mass against flipper length. Each point represents one penguin, and the fitted lines show the linear relationship within each species.

ggplot(
  analysis_data,
  aes(
    x = flipper_length_mm,
    y = body_mass_g,
    color = species
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Flipper Length and Body Mass",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Relationship between flipper length and body mass by penguin species.






round(cor(analysis_data$flipper_length_mm, analysis_data$body_mass_g), 2)

[1] 0.87

title: Flipper Length and Body Mass in Penguins
text:
Findings
The summary statistics and figure show a positive relationship between flipper length and body mass in the Palmer Penguins data. Penguins with longer flippers generally have greater body mass.
Across all penguins the correlation between flipper length and body mass is strong (about 0.87), but part of that comes from Gentoos being larger on both measures. Within each species the relationship is still positive but weaker: about 0.47 for Adelie, 0.64 for Chinstrap and 0.70 for Gentoo (Table 1, Figure 1).
These results are descriptive and summarize the observations in this dataset. They do not establish that flipper length causes differences in body mass.

title: Flipper Length and Body Mass in Penguins
text:
Conclusion
Using R, I loaded the Palmer Penguins dataset, inspected its structure, removed observations with missing values for the variables of interest, calculated species-level summaries and correlations, and created a visualization of the relationship between flipper length and body mass.
The analysis demonstrates a reproducible R workflow because the data processing, calculations, and figure are generated from code when the Quarto document is rendered.
